# Education in China – Concise Summary
China’s education system is built upon a foundation of nine years of compulsory education, which includes six years of primary school and three years of junior secondary (middle) school. The government prioritizes universal literacy, with targeted policies for rural and urban areas and special provisions for disadvantaged and minority populations. The curriculum at all levels emphasizes core subjects such as Chinese, mathematics, and moral/political education (with Communist Party values integrated throughout). Senior secondary (high school) and higher education are competitive, with admissions determined by high-stakes entrance examinations (Zhongkao for high school and Gaokao for university). Vocational and technical education are also promoted, but general academic tracks remain favored.
Key challenges persist, including regional and gender disparities, resource gaps between urban and rural schools, and a rigorous, exam-oriented approach which can hinder creativity and holistic development. The government has implemented reforms to address homework and private tutoring burdens and has taken steps to close for-profit private schools. Advances have been made in ICT integration, online education, and teacher training, and China’s higher education sector is now the world’s largest, with increasing international reputation. Adult education, special education, and supplemental learning opportunities (including distance and online education) play significant roles in lifelong learning and workforce development. Though China’s top students and select regions regularly excel in international assessments, inequality and access issues remain a central concern.
